sources.text:
Finnish personal identity code: get a henkilötunnus | Hello Expat

# Finnish personal identity code: how to get a henkilötunnus and a tax card

By The Hello Expat editorial team· Updated on 21 October 2026· 6 min read· How we check

In this article

1. What is the Finnish personal identity code?
2. Who can get a Finnish personal identity code?
3. How do you register at the DVV step by step?
4. How do you get a Finnish tax card?
5. What if you need to start work before you have the code?
6. What can you do without a personal identity code?
7. How is the Finnish personal identity code used day to day?
8. How does the process differ for family members and children?
9. What changes if you are British or on Åland?
10. What are the common mistakes?

In Finland, almost every form eventually asks for the same thing: eleven characters that start with your birthday. Your doctor wants it, your landlord wants it, your employer wants it, and the bank will not give you online codes without it. Getting your Finnish personal identity code, the henkilötunnus, is the single most important step of your first month.

The good news is that the process is free and well documented. The less good news is that you must go in person.

## What is the Finnish personal identity code?

The henkilötunnus is the identifier of the Finnish population information system. It is made up of your date of birth, a sign for the century, and an individual ending with a check character. It is issued when you are entered in the population information system, usually by the Digi- ja väestötietovirasto (DVV, the Digital and Population Data Services Agency). In some cases Migri, when registering your right of residence, or the Tax Administration can issue one as well; Vero says so on its page for people arriving in Finland.

Do not confuse it with the veronumero, the tax number. The tax number matters only in construction and shipbuilding, where you must register at a tax office and cannot enter the site without it. Everybody else works with the henkilötunnus.

## Who can get a Finnish personal identity code?

You must be legally resident in Finland and have a ground for needing one. The DVV lists these examples:

- you work in Finland with the right to work;
- you study in Finland;
- you are a family member of someone who already has a registered Finnish address;
- you hold a residence permit, a residence card or an EU registration certificate.

For an EU citizen staying more than three months, the Migri registration is the proof of lawful residence. See residence in Finland for EU citizens for that step. Nordic citizens go directly to the DVV. Swiss and Liechtenstein citizens follow the same route as EU citizens.

## How do you register at the DVV step by step?

1. Fill in the online form. It is the "Registration Information of a Foreigner" form. You do not need electronic identification, and a paper form exists.
2. Book an appointment. The DVV requires a visit in person. You must come within one month of submitting the form, and children come too.
3. Bring your documents: a valid passport or EU/EEA identity card, your Migri EU registration certificate or residence document, proof of work or studies (a contract or a school certificate), and, if you claim family ties, civil-status certificates, legalised and translated where required.
4. State your language. Tell the DVV whether you want service in Finnish or Swedish.
5. Ask for a municipality of residence on the same form if you stay at least a year.
6. Wait. The identity code is issued 2 to 3 weeks after the visit if you work or study, and 3 to 4 weeks otherwise.

The same form can be used for children under 18 who arrive with you. International House centres in Helsinki, Joensuu, Oulu, Rauma, Tampere and Turku (and International Pointti in Kemi) pull several agencies under one roof, and the DVV is present in them. They are worth knowing if your first appointment needs help in English.

Not sure which of your certificates need legalising, or which line to tick on the form? Moovy can walk through your situation, list the documents and draft the Finnish or Swedish note you take to the counter.

## How do you get a Finnish tax card?

Once you have your henkilötunnus, you apply to Verohallinto (Vero, the Tax Administration) for a verokortti, the tax card. Vero says that applying for one requires a Finnish personal identity code. If a visit is needed, Vero gives you an appointment. Processing normally takes one to three working days when all information is available.

Prepare an estimate of your income for the whole year, because the tax card carries a withholding percentage and an income ceiling. Give a copy to your employer. One card works for all your employers, with a single annual ceiling.

## What if you need to start work before you have the code?

Ask Vero or the DVV for the code in the same visit as your tax card application. Some tax offices in large cities can issue an identity code at the same time. If you start anyway without a tax card, your employer withholds 60 per cent of your salary. It comes back later through the tax return, but your cash flow suffers in the meantime.

## What can you do without a personal identity code?

You can open a bank account, though banks may not issue full online banking codes without the code. You can buy a prepaid SIM card without giving an identifier. You can receive urgent medical care, and you may be billed afterwards if you have no entitlement. What you cannot do: get a tax card, apply to Kela, sign a regular phone subscription, or use most public online services. Read Kela in Finland for the benefits side.

## How is the Finnish personal identity code used day to day?

Everywhere. Your employer reports your pay under it. Your bank links your account to it. Kela, Vero and your municipality identify you with it. When you book a doctor, the health centre asks for it; when you sign a lease, many landlords ask for it. The Kanta services, where you view prescriptions and test results, are tied to it as well.

That is also why Finns treat it carefully. It is not a secret in the way a password is, but it is a key to your records. Do not post it on social media, do not send it by email to someone you have not verified, and be suspicious of any message that claims to be from Vero or Kela and asks you to click a link. Vero warns on its own site that scam messages have been sent in its name.

## How does the process differ for family members and children?

Children under 18 who arrive with you are registered on the same DVV form and attend the visit with you. A child born in Finland must be registered with Migri within three months of birth if the child needs EU registration. Family certificates issued outside the Nordic countries and the EU must be legalised, and translated if they are not in Finnish, Swedish or English. If you rely on a family tie to the person who already has a registered address, the DVV will want to see the certificate that proves it. Bring originals, not photocopies, because the DVV checks the originals.

## What changes if you are British or on Åland?

British citizens are third-country nationals since Brexit. With a residence permit, registration in the population system is automatic and the identity code is issued at the same time. See moving to Finland from the UK.

On Åland, the same identity code system applies, but a state office in Mariehamn (Statens ämbetsverk på Åland) does the DVV's counter work, and a foreigner must register in person.

## What are the common mistakes?

- Starting work before the tax card. Plan the DVV appointment first.
- Mixing up the henkilötunnus and the veronumero.
- Forgetting that registration at the DVV is separate from Migri. You need both.
- Moving house without telling the DVV. Every change of address is declared there, free of charge.
- Staying under a year and expecting a municipality of residence.

Once the code arrives, guard it. Combined with your name it unlocks a lot, and you should never share it in an email or message to someone you cannot identify.

To see all your admin steps for moving to Finland, in order and with their official sources, go to Hello Expat's Finland page.

## Frequently asked questions

What is a Finnish personal identity code?+

The henkilötunnus is an 11-character identifier built from your date of birth and a personal ending. Banks, employers, Kela, Vero and healthcare providers use it. You receive it when you are registered in the population information system.

How long does it take to get a henkilötunnus?+

The DVV says 2 to 3 weeks if you came to work or study and 3 to 4 weeks in other cases. The count starts on the day of your visit to the DVV.

Is the Finnish personal identity code free?+

Yes. Registration with the DVV and the code itself are free. If you are an EU citizen staying more than three months, the earlier Migri registration costs €53 in 2026.

Can I work in Finland without a tax card?+

Yes, but your employer then withholds 60 per cent of your pay. The excess is returned later, but it is a real cash-flow problem in your first months.

Is the henkilötunnus the same as the Finnish tax number?+

No. In practice the tax number (veronumero) is only for construction and shipyard work, where you must register at a tax office. Everyone else uses the henkilötunnus.

Streamlined services for issuing personal identity codes and municipality of residence for foreign citizens - Finnish Government

# Streamlined services for issuing personal identity codes and municipality of residence for foreign citizens

 Publication date 28.4.2025 10.45 

The Digital and Population Data Services Agency took action last year in order to streamline the registration of foreigners. You can now get your personal identity code when visiting the agency in 12 locations. The updated website and instructional videos will guide customers to use services that match their situation.

The registration of foreigners' personal data has accelerated as the Digital and Population Data Services Agency has improved its practices and systems. You can now apply for a personal identity code and municipality of residence online, which speeds up processing and improves the accuracy of the data. After filling in the online form, the customer must still usually visit the agency in order to verify their identity.

“Data registration is much faster than before. We are now able to provide a personal identity code and a municipality of residence during a visit, provided the conditions are met,” says Maisa Gynther, Chief Specialist at the Digital and Population Data Services Agency.

“We are thrilled to make the everyday lives of our foreign customers easier by granting them a personal identity code and a municipality of residence quickly. This has been the result of several years of development,” Gynther adds.

## Customers can receive their personal identity code in connection to a visit 

A few service locations of the Digital and Population Data Services Agency tested the practice first and started issuing a personal identity code during a personal visit, and as their experiences were positive, the practice was adopted permanently. At the moment, persons who have booked an appointment and completed an online form may receive their personal identity code in 12 locations: Helsinki, Joensuu, Jyväskylä, Kuopio, Lahti, Lappeenranta, Oulu, Pori, Rovaniemi, Tampere, Turku and Vaasa. 

To receive their personal identity code during the visit, the customer must first submit their data to the Digital and Population Data Services Agency using an online form and book an appointment online. They must also meet the requirements for obtaining a personal identity code. However, a personal identity code cannot always be issued during a visit if the matter requires further clarification. 

The online form for obtaining a personal identity code is available to all foreigners, and it does not require strong identification. You can use the same form to request a municipality of residence if you are intending to stay in Finland for more than one year. The conditions for obtaining a personal identity code and municipality of residence are examined individually for each customer.

## Obtaining a personal identity code and municipality of residence faster make the daily life of foreigners easier

Having a Finnish personal identity code makes many everyday matters possible, such as dealing with the authorities, opening a bank account and receiving wages. In addition to the Digital and Population Data Services Agency, a foreigner may in certain situations receive a personal identity code from the Tax Administration or the Finnish Immigration Service.

You can also apply for a municipality of residence online if you have a personal identity code and you fulfil the statutory requirements for obtaining a municipality of residence. Often, you must also visit the Digital and Population Data Services Agency in person to obtain a municipality of residence. You do not have to apply for a municipality of residence, but you need it to get a Finnish identity card or a student discount for public transport, for example. 

## The website instructs customers what to do in their situation

Several changes have been made to the Digital and Population Data Services Agency’s dvv.fi website to improve the user experience. Thanks to a clearer website, foreigners can find the right instructions for their situation more easily than before. By answering the questions on the website, the customer can move towards the right way to use services. The new instructional videos also help customers to apply for a personal identity code and a municipality of residence.

 For additional information and instructional videos, visit https://dvv.fi/en/as-a-foreigner-in-finland 

Additional information: Chief Specialist Maisa Gynther, Digital and Population Data Services Agency, tel. +358 295 536 355, [email protected]. 

### Finnish Government

Snellmaninkatu 1 A, Helsinki

PO Box 23, FI-00023 Government, Finland

Tel. +358 295 16001

How Long Does It Take to Get a Personal Identity Code in Finland? - Finland Handbook

# How Long Does It Take to Get a Personal Identity Code in Finland?

 By Finland Handbook Editorial Team June 12, 2026 November 6, 2026 November 6, 2026 

One of the most frustrating "chicken and egg" loops in Finland is trying to open a bank account or sign a rental agreement only to be told you need a Personal Identity Code, while being told by the authorities that the code is currently "in processing." I remember sitting in a cold waiting room in Pasila, clutching my passport and wondering if I’d ever actually exist in the Finnish system. This guide will clarify exactly how long the wait is and how to navigate the administrative silence.

Table of Contents

## Understanding the Personal Identity Code Timelines by Application Path

The time it takes to receive your henkilötunnus (Personal Identity Code) depends almost entirely on which "door" you use to enter the Finnish system. There isn't one single office that handles everyone; rather, your path is determined by your citizenship and your reason for moving. The Finnish Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV) has streamlined many digital aspects, but physical identity verification remains a bottleneck that dictates the total duration of your wait.

If you are a non-EU citizen applying for your first residence permit from abroad, you usually request the code as part of your permit application. In this scenario, the code is issued simultaneously with your residence permit. This means your "wait time" for the code is essentially the wait time for your permit, which can range from a few weeks for specialists to several months for family-based ties. The moment you receive your residence permit card, the code is printed on the back. This is by far the most efficient route, as it bypasses the need for a separate visit to the DVV once you land.

However, for EU citizens or those who didn't receive a code with their permit, the process involves a visit to the DVV. In 2026, the standard processing time for a Personal Identity Code at the DVV is generally 1 to 3 weeks after your appointment. The real challenge is often securing the appointment itself. In major cities like Helsinki, Espoo, or Tampere, the "wait for the wait" can be significant. You might find that the first available slot for identity verification is three weeks away, and only after that does the 1–3 week processing clock begin. Understanding Getting Your Personal Identity Code: The Key to Finnish Healthcare is essential here, as this code is the bedrock of your entire administrative life in Finland.

| Application Path | Typical Processing Time | Key Requirement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Residence Permit (Migri) | Linked to permit (1–6 months) | Applied for abroad or at Migri |
| EU Citizen (DVV) | 1–3 weeks after appointment | Valid passport & proof of work/study |
| Nordic Citizen (DVV) | 1 week | Personal appearance at DVV |
| Temporary Worker (Short-term) | 1–2 weeks | Finnish employer's confirmation |

## Factors That Impact the Speed of Your Registration

While the official estimates give a baseline, the reality on the ground in Finland can vary based on seasonal demand. The "August Rush" is a very real phenomenon. Every year, thousands of international students and new hires arrive simultaneously in late summer. If you submit your request in August or early September, expect the DVV processing times to stretch toward the 4-to-6-week mark. Many newcomers get caught in this cycle, struggling to get their electricity contracts or home internet because the system is simply overwhelmed by the volume of new residents.

Another major factor is the completeness of your documentation. The Finnish authorities are meticulous. If you are moving based on family ties, for example, and your marriage certificate or your child’s birth certificate lacks the proper apostille or legalisation, the DVV will pause your application. They won't necessarily tell you immediately; your file might just sit in a "pending" queue until a clerk reviews it and sends a request for clarification. This can add weeks to the process. Always ensure your documents are translated into Finnish, Swedish, or English by an authorized translator before your appointment.

Furthermore, your location in Finland matters. While Helsinki is the hub, it is also the most congested. If you have the flexibility to travel, sometimes booking an appointment at a DVV office in a smaller town like Porvoo, Lahti, or even further afield can shave weeks off your wait for an appointment. Once the identity verification is done, the digital processing time is relatively uniform across the country, but getting that face-to-face meeting is the primary hurdle. Many people overlook how critical this step is when Registering Your Move (Muuttoilmoitus) with DVV and Posti to ensure their address is correctly linked to their new code.

## Navigating Life and Health Without a Code

The most pressing question for most is: what do I do while I wait? It feels like life is on hold. You cannot easily get a Finnish bank account, which in turn means you cannot get "Strong Electronic Identification" (bank IDs) to log into government services. During this gap, you are in a state of administrative limbo. For everyday needs, you can often use your foreign passport for basic things, but for services like healthcare, it becomes tricky. Public health centers usually require a Personal Identity Code to create a patient record in their digital systems.

If you fall ill during this waiting period, you might wonder Can I See a Doctor in Finland Before I Get a Municipality of Residence? The answer is yes, but it is often more complicated and expensive. Without the code and the subsequent "Municipality of Residence" (kotikunta) status, you are often billed at the full cost of care rather than the subsidized resident rate. This is where having private bridge insurance is a lifesaver. Companies like Cigna Global or SafetyWing are popular choices for expats who are caught in the "waiting for DVV" phase. These providers allow you to access private clinics like Terveystalo or Mehiläinen without needing a Finnish ID code.

While waiting for your code, SafetyWing can provide travel-medical style coverage that handles emergencies, while Cigna Global offers more comprehensive annual plans that cover you while you are still invisible to the Finnish Kela system. Using private care during these first few weeks is often the only way to avoid the stress of navigating the public system without a code. It’s also worth noting that until you have that code, you won't be able to easily use Omakanta and the Kanta Services: Finland's Digital Health Records and Prescriptions, as these require Finnish bank IDs to log in. Keeping your private insurance details handy is the best way to ensure you aren't left stranded.

## Practical Steps to Speed Up the Process

To ensure you get your code as fast as possible, you need to be proactive rather than reactive. The moment you know your move-in date, or the moment you receive your residence permit, check the DVV’s online booking system. Do not wait until you land in Finland to see what’s available. Appointments fill up weeks in advance. If you see no appointments in Helsinki, widen your search radius. The train system in Finland is excellent, and a one-hour trip to a neighboring town could save you three weeks of waiting in the city.

When you attend your appointment, bring every possible document that proves your right to be in Finland. This includes your passport, your residence permit card (if applicable), your employment contract, or your certificate of attendance from a university. For EU citizens, proving your "right of residence" often requires showing that you have sufficient funds or a job. If the clerk has everything they need in one go, your application can be processed in the "fast track" queue. If they have to ask for more info, you go back to the bottom of the pile.

Once you have your code, your next step is often Getting Your Personal Identity Code: The Key to Finnish Healthcare by ensuring your municipality of residence is also registered. The code itself is just a string of numbers; the status attached to it (whether you are a permanent resident or a temporary visitor) determines your rights to Kela benefits and public healthcare. If you are a student, for example, you should clarify Can I Use Finnish Healthcare on a Student Residence Permit? as your access level might differ from someone on a permanent work contract. Once the code arrives via post or email, treat it like gold—it is the master key to your new life.

## Managing Your Healthcare Transition

As you wait for the administrative wheels to turn, it's vital to have a plan for your prescriptions and ongoing health needs. Many expats make the mistake of assuming they can just walk into a pharmacy with a foreign prescription and get their meds. In Finland, pharmacies generally require a Finnish electronic prescription. Until you have your Personal Identity Code and can be entered into the system, getting a Finnish doctor to issue that prescription is your first priority. Again, this is where private providers like Cigna Global or SafetyWing facilitate faster access to private doctors who can bridge that gap for you.

Once you finally receive your code, you can begin the process of Healthcare in Finland for Foreign Residents: The Complete System Guide (2027). This involves registering at your local terveysasema (health station). Don't expect this to happen automatically. Even after the DVV gives you a code, you often need to proactively contact your local wellbeing services county to ensure you are in their database. This is a common point of confusion: the DVV manages your identity, but the Wellbeing Services County manages your health access.

Finally, keep in mind that the Personal Identity Code is also the prerequisite for applying for a Kela card. You can read more about this in Kela Explained: Health Insurance, Reimbursements, and Your Kela Card. Without the ID code, Kela cannot process your application for social security coverage. If you are working, your employer will also need this code to pay your salary and handle your tax withholdings correctly. It truly is the "linchpin" of the Finnish system. While the 1-to-3-week wait might feel like an eternity when you're trying to settle in, being prepared with private insurance like SafetyWing or Cigna Global ensures that your health and safety aren't compromised by a bit of bureaucratic lag.

Location: Wyoming, USA | Email: contact@choismedia.com

DVV registration in Finland is how a foreigner enters the Population Information System and receives a henkilötunnus (personal identity code) that banks, the tax office and Kela rely on. The registration is for people who are genuinely settling in for a meaningful period, not for tourists or very short visits. If you need the code for tax reasons when you start working in Finland, a tax office can also issue a personal identity code — but that alone does not give you a municipality of residence. ...

### Step 2 — Book an in-person appointment within one month

After the form, you must visit a DVV service point in person, and you must do so within one month of submitting. The in-person step is non-negotiable — it is where DVV verifies your identity against your documents. Appointments at the busy Helsinki-area locations can fill up, so book as early as you can rather than leaving it to the end of the one-month window.

...

### Step 4 — Wait for processing

Processing time, according to DVV, is roughly 2–3 weeks for work and study registrations and 3–4 weeks for other cases, counted from your visit date. At the end you receive your personal identity code, and DVV separately decides your municipality of residence.

...

DVV operates service points across Finland — major cities including Helsinki, Tampere, Turku, and Oulu have offices, and there are around a dozen physical locations nationally. You can also reach DVV by telephone on +358 295 536 320 (Mon–Fri 9–15) and through secure email for questions about your case.

...

## A Realistic Timeline for Your First Month

Putting it together, a typical sequence for a new arrival looks like this:

1. Before or on arrival — settle your residence basis with Migri (permit for non-EU; right-of-residence registration for EU citizens staying over three months).
2. First days — submit the DVV foreigner registration form online and book the in-person appointment.
3. Within the first month — attend the DVV appointment with your documents; this is also a good moment to use International House Helsinki if you are in the capital region.
4. Weeks two to four — DVV processes the registration (2–3 weeks for work/study, 3–4 weeks otherwise) and assigns your personal identity code and, where eligible, your municipality of residence.
5. Once you have the henkilötunnus — open a Finnish bank account, order a tax card from Vero, and register with Kela.
6. Whenever you move permanently or for over 3 months — file a notification of move within one week.

The order matters because each step depends on the one before it. The single most useful thing you can do is start the DVV form early and book the appointment immediately, since the in-person slot is usually the bottleneck. Everything downstream — banking, tax, healthcare — is waiting on the code DVV gives you at the end.

sources.title: Personal identity code in Finland - Herizon
highlights:
As a foreign citizen you get a Finnish personal identity code (henkilötunnus) by registering with the Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV): you submit its form, then visit a DVV service point in person within one month. DVV's registration page states: "Everyone who requests a personal identity code must visit in person within 1 month of submitting the form, including children." Registration is free of charge, and DVV processes a request based on work or study in 2 to 3 weeks counted from the day of your visit. The code alone does not give you a municipality of residence (kotikunta), which is a separate decision with its own conditions.

...

1. Fill in the form. DVV's online form "does not require authentication". One parent can request a code on the same form for a child under 18 who moves to Finland at the same time.
2. Book the visit at once. Book your appointment through DVV's registration page. The one-month clock starts on the day you submit the form, so book in the same sitting.
3. Bring the documents. DVV lists a valid passport or an official photo ID card (for EU, EEA and certain other nationals); a residence permit card or other proof that you reside legally in Finland; the EU registration certificate if you have one; and proof of work or studies, "for example, a certificate of student status or an employment contract".

...

Add family documents if needed. If you also register a marriage or parenthood, bring the completed forms and the certificates, legalised and translated where DVV's rules require it.

DVV's registration page sets these processing times and fee:

| Request | Processing time | Price |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Code request based on work or study | 2 to 3 weeks from the visit | Free |
| Code request on other grounds | 3 to 4 weeks from the visit | Free |

...

Take a non-EU specialist with a continuous (A) residence permit. The DVV form goes in, the appointment is booked within the month, and the passport, permit card and employment contract go to the visit. DVV states the code takes 2 to 3 weeks from the visit for work-based requests. A municipality of residence may be granted at the same time if DVV's conditions are met, which an A permit satisfies when the person also intends to stay at least a year. The tax card can be applied for once the code exists, as the Tax Administration requires it.

...

### How long does it take to get a personal identity code in Finland?

DVV's registration page gives 2 to 3 weeks for a request based on work or study and 3 to 4 weeks for other grounds. The clock starts on the day of your in-person visit, so a late appointment delays the code.

sources.title: Henkilötunnus and DVV registration
highlights:
If Migri (Finnish Immigration Service; Migrationsverket in Swedish) grants you a residence permit, a residence card or EU registration and a Finnish authority verified your identity, the code comes with the decision; if you proved your identity at a VFS centre abroad, you book a DVV appointment after arrival. Otherwise you go to DVV, or – for tax purposes only – to a tax office.

| Route | Who | How | Time and cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Automatically from Migri | Anyone granted a residence permit, residence card or EU registration, identity verified by a Finnish authority | Nothing to do; the code arrives with the decision | No separate fee |
| DVV | Everyone else residing legally with grounds: work, studies, a family member with a registered address, or a Migri decision; all children | Online form without login, then a visit within one month – every person, children included | Free; 2–3 weeks for work or study, 3–4 weeks for others |
| Tax office | Workers who need a code only for a tax card or tax number | Form 6150e plus 5057e or 5042e; appointment on 029 497 010 | Usually 1–3 business days; only Helsinki Pasila, Kuopio, Oulu, Rovaniemi, Seinäjoki, Tampere, Turku and Mariehamn; not for children under 15 |

Source: DVV, Migri and the Finnish Tax Administration, read 24 September 2026.

sources.title: Finnish Personal Identity Code (Henkilötunnus) Guide | NordicExpat
highlights:
Take with you:

- Valid passport or official EU/EEA photo ID card.
- Residence permit card (non-EU) or EU registration certificate — or proof you have applied for one.
- Proof of legal grounds for staying: employment contract, study acceptance/enrolment certificate, or equivalent.
- Proof of a Finnish address if you have it: a rental agreement, or confirmation from your employer or university.
- For family relationships, bring legalised and translated certificates (marriage, birth) where relevant.

...

This is the single most common misunderstanding, so treat it as a separate fact: having a henkilötunnus is not the same as having a municipality of residence (kotikunta — "home municipality"). The personal identity code identifies you; the kotikunta status is what entitles you to subsidised municipal and wellbeing-county services — most importantly public healthcare at standard client fees, and day care.

Both DVV and Migri are explicit that getting a code does not automatically give you a kotikunta. You apply for the municipality of residence separately with DVV, and eligibility depends on factors like the nature and length of your stay. If you register in person with DVV, raise the kotikunta question at the same appointment so you do not leave thinking you are covered for healthcare when you are not. For the wider registration picture, see our guide to registering with DVV.

...

A henkilötunnus is the key that turns on the rest of the system. With it you can:

- Open a bank account at a Finnish bank (Nordea, OP, S-Pankki, Danske Bank). See opening a bank account in Finland.
- Get a tax card (verokortti) through OmaVero / vero.fi — covered in our Finnish tax card guide.
- Register with Kela for social insurance and the Kela card, where eligible.
- Use Suomi.fi, the public services portal, once you have strong e-identification.
- Obtain online bank credentials (pankkitunnukset) — the de-facto national e-ID for logging into government and banking services.
- Access public healthcare at a health centre (terveyskeskus) — provided you also have a kotikunta.
- Enrol children in school or day care.

...

## Common Problems and Fixes

- "My permit was granted but I never got a code." Automatic issuance needs your identity to have been verified by a Finnish authority and your details to match your passport exactly. If it did not happen, request the code from DVV in person after you arrive — do not wait for it to appear on its own.
- "I have a henkilötunnus but the health centre says I'm not covered." You almost certainly have the code but not a kotikunta. Apply for the municipality of residence with DVV; until then, non-emergency public care may not be available at subsidised rates.
- "My name is spelled wrong / my date of birth is incorrect." Errors trace back to the source documents and identity check. Contact DVV to correct registered details; in narrow cases the code itself can be changed (e.g. wrong date of birth recorded).
- "I couldn't get a DVV appointment within a month of submitting the form." Appointment availability varies by city and season. Book as early as you can; if slots are scarce, check service points in nearby municipalities and the booking system at different times of day.
- "A bank refused me because I only have a foreigner's identity number." That is expected — it is not a full henkilötunnus. Use a Wise or Revolut account as interim banking, and apply for the full code once you qualify.

sources.title: Moving to Finland: Tax Card & Verokortti - Full Guide 2026
highlights:
### Tax Card (Verokortti)

Tax Card (Verokortti) in Finland: Set up before your first payday, without a tax card, your employer must apply a high default withholding rate. Your Finnish tax card (verokortti), managed through MyTax (OmaVero), tells your employer the correct withholding rate for your salary. Employees who already have a Finnish personal identity code do not need to visit a Vero service point in person to obtain a tax card, it can be requested via MyTax once your identity code is active. International experts and key employees may be eligible for special source-tax arrangements.

Finnish Tax Administration (Verohallinto, Vero)

Deadline: Set up before your first payday, without a tax card, your employer must apply a high default withholding rate.

Processing Time: Tax cards requested via MyTax (OmaVero) are typically issued immediately or within a short processing time once your personal identity code is active.

💰 Fees: Free.

📅 Appointment: Not required if you have a personal identity code, request your tax card online via MyTax (vero.fi). Without a personal identity code, a visit to a Vero service point may be necessary.

Required Documents:

- Personal identity code
- Online banking codes or a mobile certificate for MyTax authentication
- Estimated annual income for setting the correct withholding percentage

Where to Do It:

Online via MyTax (OmaVero) at vero.fi, or in person at a Vero service point if you do not yet have a personal identity code.

If You Don't Do It: Without an active tax card, your employer must withhold tax at a higher default rate than your actual liability, meaning you receive less in each paycheque until the tax card is set up and any overpayment is reconciled in your annual tax assessment.
